paragraphs.source_en: For a while I had eyes only for this old man; not only did I forget all the other monsters completely, I even forgot my master, crouching miserably in the bath and scalded by the heat. Just then, someone suddenly raised a loud voice at the boundary between the washing area and the boarded floor. When I looked, it was none other than my master, Mr. Kushami. My master's voice is exceptionally loud and hoarse, and hard to listen to; that is nothing new, of course, but in such a place it startled me more than a little. In that instant I judged that he must have stayed too long in the hot water and become flushed in the head. If it had simply been a morbid impulse, there would be no blaming him; yet even while flushed, he was plainly in full possession of himself, as will be clear enough once I explain why he let out such an outrageous bellow. He had begun, quite childishly, to quarrel with a conceited student scarcely worth noticing. It was my master, of course, who shouted, “Move farther back! You must not splash water into my little tub!” Things may be viewed in many ways, so there is no need to conclude that my master's roar was necessarily the result of his head being overheated. One might interpret it by allowing that among ten thousand men there may be one who rebukes a bandit as Takayama Hikokuro did, and Kushami himself may have been performing the scene in just that spirit. But since his opponent did not take himself for a bandit, the expected result was naturally not forthcoming. The student turned around and answered quite meekly, “I was here first.” It was an ordinary answer, indicating only that he did not intend to leave the spot and would not do as my master wished. Judging from the student's manner and tone, there was really no possibility that he deserved to be abused as a bandit. By rights, however overheated my master was, he ought to have understood that much. But my master's roaring was not because he objected to the student's position; rather, these two young men had been saying nothing but offensively arrogant, knowing things, quite unbefitting their years, and having listened to it all along, my master had clearly flown into a rage on that account. Therefore, even though the other party replied politely, my master would not quietly go back up onto the boarded floor. At this, my master thundered again, “What, you idiot! Who ever heard of splashing filthy water into another man's tub?” I too had felt some resentment toward these young fellows, so at that moment I could not help crying bravo in my heart. Still, I also thought that such words and behavior were hardly proper for my master, who was a schoolteacher. To begin with, my master is too rigid by nature, and that is no good. He is like spent coal cinders: all sharp edges, dry and brittle, and most unpleasantly hard. They say that long ago, when Hannibal crossed the Alps, a huge rock blocked the middle of the road and impeded the passage of his army; so Hannibal poured vinegar over the rock, built a fire against it to soften it, and then sawed a great section from the middle of it, allowing the army to pass without difficulty.

units.source_zh: 据说在古时候汉尼拔在越过阿尔卑斯山时，在进军路上有一巨大岩石阻路，妨碍军队通过，于是汉尼拔在这块岩石上浇上醋，然后用火烤，使岩石松软，然后用锯从中间将这块巨岩锯去了一大节，于是军队得以顺利通过。

paragraphs.source_zh: 我暂时只顾注意这老头儿，不但把其他怪物们都忘得一干二净，而且把蹲在浴池里烫得难受的主人也给忘到九霄云外去了。就在这时，突然有人在冲澡的交界处大声喊叫。我一看，他不是别人而正是主人苦沙弥先生。主人的声音极大而且沙哑，不易听清，这当然不是从今天才这样的，不过，这次是在这样的地方，所以惹得我特别吃惊。我匆忙中想到这准是主人在热水池里浸泡得时间太长、虚火上升的缘故。这件事，如果单纯是他的病态冲动，当然不能责备他，然而他虽虚火上升，头脑却分明十分清醒，这点只要说明他为什么发出如此离了谱儿的大喊大叫，就可以了解。他是同一个不值得理睬的自高自大的“书生”争吵起来的。主人在喊叫：“你给我往后退！往我的小桶里溅水可不行！”事物是多种多样的，没有必要一定认为主人的狂叫是由于虚火上升。您可以这样解释，在一万个人当中允许有个人像高山彦九郎那样来大声斥骂山贼，而苦沙弥本人也许正是以这样的意图来演出这出戏的。不过，对手既然不以山贼自任，当然不会出现预想的结果。那个“书生”回过头来，很老实地说道：“是我先在这里的。”这是一般的回答，只表示他不想离开那个位置，不肯照主人的想法办。从“书生”的态度和语气来看，实在没有被值得骂为山贼的可能。按理说，不管主人怎样虚火上升，这点也是应该明白的。但是，主人的这番狂叫并不是对“书生”占据的位置不满，而是完全因为刚才这两个青年人毫无那种稳当劲儿，一味地讲了许多高傲自大、自作聪明的事儿，主人听了这些大动肝火。所以对方只是老老实实地回答了一句，并不想退回到板地上来。这样，主人又大喝了一声：“什么，混蛋！你怎么可以把脏水哗啦哗啦往别人的小桶里溅呢？”我心里对这两个小青年早就不满了，这时也不由得喊了声“快哉！”不过，我又觉得作为学校教师的主人，他的这一言行也不够妥当。说起来，主人性格总是过于古板，不太好。他就像烧过的煤渣一样，全是棱角，而且又死硬得很。据说在古时候汉尼拔在越过阿尔卑斯山时，在进军路上有一巨大岩石阻路，妨碍军队通过，于是汉尼拔在这块岩石上浇上醋，然后用火烤，使岩石松软，然后用锯从中间将这块巨岩锯去了一大节，于是军队得以顺利通过。
